diagnosis: Adds both the numerators and the denominators together instead of keeping the denominator the same.
rationale: The learner correctly added 2 + 1 to get 3, but also added the denominators 5 + 5 to get 10. A number-line demonstration partitioned into fifths clearly shows that adding fifths means hopping along fifths, keeping the unit denominator unchanged.

script.focus: the tick marks stay fifths as you hop forward

intent: Demonstrate add on the number-line with values [1,3] (unit 1/5). Tutor points at: the tick marks stay fifths as you hop forward

frames.caption: Start at 1/5. We are standing here; we have not hopped yet.
Hop 1 moves 1/5 forward and lands on 2/5. One hop is one fifth.
Hop 3 lands on 4/5. 3 hops, so 1/5 + 3/5 = 4/5. Every hop was one fifth; the size of the pieces never changed, only how many.

judgement.reasoning: The demonstration directly addresses the misconception of adding denominators by showing hops on a fifths number line where the denominator stays 5. It switches from a fraction bar to a number line representation, is passive and easier (worked demonstration), stays within 4th-grade fractions, and uses 1/5 + 3/5 instead of the student's problem 2/5 + 1/5.
judgement.verdict: Yes, this worked demonstration effectively uses a number line to show that moving by fifths keeps the denominator unchanged.
